28_marg452: He that oppresseth, etc. It is clear that the rapacious lose both what they take from the poor and what they seemed to possess justly, when in the judgement they receive punishment for what they did.
28_marg453: Incline, etc. Thus far the title of the parables of Solomon, which was set above, from which point it is shown to speak in a new manner, not to one whom he teaches but reasoning with himself; which began there: A wise son maketh a glad father, and ends here: shall himself give to one that is richer, and shall be in need. From here he returns to the former manner of speaking, so as to address his words to him whom he teaches: Incline thy ear, etc. A beautiful beginning of the new discourse, that the hearer should open his ear to hear and set his heart to understand what the wise say.
28_interl1415: in this book he teaches us to practise it in thought, speech and deed
28_interl1416: to anyone, but above all to Christ, who became poor for us
28_interl1417: “To thee is the poor man left: thou wilt be a helper to the orphan.”
28_marg454: Be not a friend, etc. Generally: as the perfect ought not to flee perverse neighbours, because they often draw them to good and are not themselves perverted by them, so the weak ought to flee the company of the wicked, lest they begin to imitate the evils they often see and cannot correct.
28_marg455: To an angry man, etc. To anyone, but above all to the Jews, who raged with insane mind against Christ and his disciples; from whose friendship those who care to be saved are forbidden, lest by their nearness they too perish; which the fall of Judas proved can happen.
28_interl1418: he does not forbid taking up the charge of government when canonically laid on one, but usurping it rashly
28_marg456: Be not with them, etc. Be not with those who, though they are free and at leisure for themselves, fasten down their hands in the cares of the salvation of the wicked, pledging that they will render account for their souls. For if he for whom thou hast pledged thyself has not the good works by which to render thee free and safe from thy pledge, what profit is it to thee that thou thyself be judged for his soul in the day of judgement, and lose the garment of justice in which thou seemedst clothed?
28_marg457: Pass not beyond, etc. Pass not beyond the bounds of the catholic faith which the doctors set from the beginning.
28_marg458: Hast thou seen a man, etc. Whomever thou seest swift in his work, that is, vigorous and careful in the good that was his to do, know that he will stand in the judgement before the apostles, who will judge with Christ, because he kept their commands; and that he is not to be set on the left hand with the obscure teachers, whose error he shunned.
28_interl1432: that is, not depraved by error
28_marg459: When thou shalt sit, etc. Allegorically. It is to be read thus: when thou shalt sit reading with the master, to be refreshed with the bread of the word, understand diligently what is written, and keep the discretion of the holy reading in thy speech, if only thou art such and so learned that thou hast thy soul in thy power. For he put the throat for speech, because the voice is in the throat; the knife for discretion, because with it we cut. He that sits to eat, then, puts a knife to his throat when he who diligently meditates on the divine utterances brings out of his mouth discreet words, and turns over on his tongue no words more often than those of the heavenly oracle. But this is for him to do who has his soul in his power, that is, who has chosen the noble state of a wise mind amid the errors of deceivers. Whence he well adds: Be not desirous of his meats.
28_marg460: Be not desirous of his meats, etc. That is, do not desire to listen to the discourses of him who deceives his hearers with the sweetness of a lie.
28_marg461: Of which above: “Pass not beyond the ancient bounds which thy fathers have set”, namely the bounds of faith and truth given by the fathers.
28_interl1436: to search out those of the Godhead
28_interl1438: because they lie open only to the citizens of heaven
28_marg462: Eat not, etc. That is, do not talk of the Scriptures with the heretic, who envies human salvation, preferring to deceive rather than be corrected; for as the soothsayer and the diviner of dreams guesses at what he does not know, so the heretic interprets as he pleases what he does not understand in the Scriptures.
28_interl1441: because he divines as he will
28_marg463: Eat, etc. Learn without fear, he says, what I say, and do what I teach; while in the things he teaches he himself has no sure faith, knowing that he invented what he teaches.
28_interl1446: the perverse teaching thou hadst learned
28_interl1448: with which thou didst humbly favour them
28_marg464: The meats, etc. The perverse meanings thou hadst learned from the heretics thou must either forsake, being corrected through repentance, or suffer punishment for them after death; and thou shalt lose the words of confession with which thou hadst thought it right to favour them humbly when they preached.
28_marg465: In the ears, etc. “Give not that which is holy to dogs; neither cast ye your pearls before swine.” As he warned thee not to listen to the teachings of the heretics, so now he warns thee not, led astray by love of vainglory, to thrust the secrets of the truth everywhere on unclean men.
28_interl1453: it is a part of sacrilege not to give to the poor the property of the poor
28_marg466: Touch not, etc. He calls the Lord the near kinsman of little ones and the fatherless, because when he was in the flesh he deigned to become the companion of the poor rather than of the rich. Otherwise “the same is Lord over all, rich unto all that call upon him”. By the fatherless and little ones we can take those of whom it is said: “See that you despise not one of these little ones that believe in me. For I say to you, that their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven.” Whoever touches their fields and bounds, that is, whoever harms their good way of life by disturbing it, does not escape the judgement of the Lord.
28_interl1455: happy would the arts be if only craftsmen judged of them
28_interl1458: “He that spareth the rod hateth his son.”
28_marg467: Let not thy heart envy, etc. If all the day, that is, if through the whole time of this life, thou shun the examples of sinners and fear the Lord, thou shalt have the hope of a blessed reward in the latter end, that is, at the end of this life. Whence in the Apocalypse: “Be thou faithful until death: and I will give thee the crown of life.”
28_marg468: Be not in the feasts, etc. To contribute flesh to eat is, in the conversation of detraction, to tell one another the vices of their neighbours. Of whose punishment he soon adds: Because they that give themselves to drinking, etc.
28_marg469: A “symbol” is a contribution, either of words, as in a council, or of money, as in the present place. They give themselves to drinking, then, who make themselves drunk on the disgrace of another’s life. To give a symbol is to contribute words in conversation, as each contributes his share of food to eat. But they that give themselves to drinking and give symbols shall be consumed, because: “Every detractor shall be rooted out.” And drowsiness shall be clothed with rags, because death will find despised and destitute of all good works the man whom here the sickness of his detraction occupied in searching out the crimes of another’s life.
28_interl1474: at the price of the body
28_interl1479: the priest who baptized thee, who taught thee from a child
28_interl1485: or: shall envy; or: shall find
28_interl1487: he who is an example to others, or the devil
28_marg470: Who hath woe, etc. He asks by way of argument for what crimes the greatest punishment is kept, and answers by reasoning: for those who through drunkenness roll down into lust. Who hath woe? he says; whose father hath woe? By woe he means eternal destruction. Whence: “Woe to that man by whom the scandal cometh.” The father of him that hath woe is the man from whom he took examples of evil, or the devil, who poured in the suggestion; of whom it is said to the Jews: “You are of your father the devil.” Who hath contentions? Who falls into pits? Contentions, because he whom drunkenness renders powerless in his senses does not keep concord. Pits, because he does not fear to fall anywhere into the wallow of all the vices who, as if insane, does not know how to distinguish between good and evil, and very often falls into the pit of which it is said: For a harlot is a deep ditch, etc. Who hath wounds without cause? Because many who have drunk too much have received through fear wounds which they suffered with no cause from the sword. Who hath redness of eyes? Because an immoderate draught of wine brings blindness to both the outward and the inward sight.
28_marg471: He does not forbid drinking wine for necessity, but lingering over wine beyond time and usefulness, and striving to empty cups. Whence Isaias: “Woe to you that are mighty to drink wine, and stout men at drunkenness.”
28_marg472: Thy eyes, etc. It is an almost natural vice, after wine, to lust in the heart after a woman, together with foulness of words.
28_interl1494: in the storms of the world
28_marg473: And thou shalt be as one sleeping, etc. They sleep in the sea who, set amid the temptations of this world, neglect to foresee the vices rushing on them like heaps of waves; and like a pilot fast asleep they lose the stern when the mind loses the zeal of watchfulness for steering the ship of the body.
28_interl1502: to the cares of the world
28_marg474: They have beaten me: the voice of one struck and sleeping. For the mind, asleep from the care of watchfulness, is beaten and feels no pain, because it does not foresee the evils that threaten. So too it does not recognize what it has done; it is drawn and does not feel, because it is led by the allurements of the vices and yet is not roused to guard itself. It wishes to wake so as to find wine again. For though, weighed down by the sleep of torpor, it does not watch to guard itself, yet it strives after the cares of the world, so as to be always drunk with pleasures.
28_marg475: Seek not to be like, etc. Do not desire to imitate those whom thou seest entangled in the vices spoken of, but take care to give thy labour to wisdom. Whence he adds: By wisdom the house shall be built.
28_interl1508: with the gifts of the virtues
28_marg476: A wise man, etc. Not every strong man is wise, but the reverse; for even if he be weak in body, if wisdom is present he overcomes all the attacks of the strong adversary, that is, the devil.
28_interl1511: high and far off because of his pride
28_marg477: Is too high, etc. The fool cannot climb to wisdom, because he lies in the lowest vices; and though in the present he thinks he knows something, in the gate, that is, at the going out of this life, he will find that it was nothing.
28_marg478: He that deviseth, etc. He makes plain whom he calls a fool: not one slow of wit, but even one who sins by thinking.
28_marg479: If thou lose hope, etc. Nothing is more detestable than despair; whoever has it loses constancy both in the common labours of this life and, what is worse, in the contest of faith.
28_interl1514: restore those who are about to fall in the contest of persecution, or who are about to perish of hunger
28_marg480: Deliver them, etc. Deliver those who are deceived by heretics, by preaching the right faith; free those who are drawn to destruction by catholics of evil life, by teaching them through the example of good works. And if thou seest any fallen or about to fall in the contest of persecution, restore them to life by exhortation; if any are about to perish of hunger or cold, restore them with food and clothing.
28_interl1517: to every man, and so to thee too
28_marg481: Eat, my son, etc. He compares the teaching of wisdom to honey and the honeycomb, because as they excel other foods, so this excels other teachings. The honey that lies ready to hand denotes the moral surface of the letter; the honeycomb, where the honey is in the wax, the allegory, where, the veil of the letter removed, the spiritual sweetness is taken with some labour and delay.
28_marg482: Lie not in wait, etc. Do not seek an occasion by which to disparage a just man; for if he falls he will soon rise again and does not repeat the evil. But the wicked so fall that they do not rise. Whence he adds: For a just man shall fall seven times in a day and shall rise again, but the wicked, etc.
28_interl1519: elsewhere: for a just man shall fall seven times in a day
28_marg483: Seven times, etc. He is called just and yet is said to fall, that is, to sin, because it concerns light sins, without which this life is not lived; for through ignorance or forgetfulness, or being taken unawares, through necessity or the frailty of the flesh, we sin every day, whether constrained or willing, and often. And yet the just man rises again, because he is just, and human frailty does not prejudice his justice. Whence, when he speaks of the just, he does not add into evil; for though it is an evil that they fall, they rise the more quickly so as not to stick fast in evil. But on the contrary: but the wicked shall fall down into evil; because when they have fallen, or, what is graver, fallen down, that is, sinned criminally, they so consent to sin that they do not repent.
28_marg484: When thy enemy shall fall, etc. Above he forbade lying in wait for the just. Now, to make thee perfect in all things, he forbids thee to mock thy enemies, even if they have sinned or met with some adversity; lest perhaps, if by the Lord’s mercy they return to repentance and become faithful friends to thee, thou be ashamed that thou once despisedst those whom divine grace had kept for life. But as far as thou canst, grieve with those who lie fallen and help them to rise; and if the effect follows the effort, thou wilt rejoice over him healed whom thou didst grieve over sick; if not, thou wilt still not lack the fruit of goodwill before God. Or thus: thou shalt not rejoice at the fall of thy enemy, lest perhaps the Lord, by this order casting thee down, humble thy pride, which without doubt displeases him, and lest, while thou fallest into sin, he come to his senses and be healed.
28_interl1521: “The things that are God’s to God.”
28_interl1522: “The things that are Caesar’s to Caesar.”
28_marg485: Fear the Lord, etc. By the Lord and the king can be understood the Father and the Son, who are to be worshipped with the same honour of Godhead. “He who honoureth not the Son, honoureth not the Father, who hath sent him,” etc. Have nothing to do with detracters: namely with those who, saying they knew God the Father, would not receive the Son of God appearing in the flesh; for their destruction shall rise suddenly, and who knoweth the ruin of both? Of both, both of the detracter and of him who favours him: of the princes who disparaged Christ and of the people deceived by them; of the heresiarchs who tear the faith and of the hearers who listen to them.
28_marg486: These things also, etc. When the reprobate are snatched from the world by a sudden destruction. Or: these things also are to be observed by the wise which I taught, that they have nothing to do with detracters, because by this vice in particular almost the whole human race is endangered. Whence Augustine at his table: “Whoever loves to pick at the life of the absent with his words, let him know this table is unworthy of him.” Another translation more plainly: These things, understand, are unknown to us who acknowledge wisdom. Which can be the beginning of what follows: It is not good to have respect to persons in judgment, etc. Above he taught us to fear the king, and now forbids respect of persons in judgement. From which it is gathered that we must so serve princes that we never depart from the way of truth through reverence or fear of them.
28_marg487: He shall kiss the lips, etc. A kiss is the sign of peace and love. He that answereth right words, then, shall kiss the lips; because whoever, disregarding respect of persons, follows only the words of justice may perhaps seem grievous and severe to the foolish, yet he will find many with whom to have peace, many prudent men who embrace his words with love, and the same men who often opposed him turned to better things.
28_marg488: Prepare thy work without, etc. To till the field diligently once the work is prepared is, when the briars of iniquity have been pulled up, to cultivate our action for the harvest of reward; and after tilling the field to build the house is that we mostly learn from good works how great a purity of life we should build up in our thoughts too. For he builds the house outwardly who first cleanses the field of the body from the thorns of the vices; lest, if the briars of the desires thrive in the field of the flesh, the whole structure of the virtues within be destroyed while the fame of good grows.
28_interl1524: do not cherish him in his sins
28_interl1526: because the reprobate neglect to do the things said before, he rightly adds: I passed by the field of the slothful man
28_marg489: To pass by the field and vineyard of the slothful and foolish is to look into the life of any negligent man, which nettles or thorns fill; because in the heart of the negligent itching earthly desires and the prickings of the vices sprout up. Whence: “Every idle man is in desires.” And the stone wall in the vineyard or field of the foolish man lies broken down when the negligent man loses the defences of the virtues he had begun, deceived either by the wickedness of men or by the persuasion of the devil.
28_marg490: These are also parables, etc. Here he begins to speak in a new order, as if drawing out, not to a hearer but with himself, what the reason of truth holds; in which, however, each may learn what he ought to shun and what to seek. These parables the men of Ezechias are said to have copied out, because until his time they were held scattered among those who had caught them as they were once spoken from Solomon’s mouth; but by his diligence they were gathered and put into this little book. Note that in these parables there are many more allegorical sayings than in the rest, drawn, namely, from the comparison of things that seem fit for figures.
28_marg491: It is the glory of the Lord appearing in the flesh to show to the eyes of mortals the nature of his manhood rather than of his Godhead, and to confess himself the Word of God, that is, the Son, by miracles and mystical sayings rather than openly. Whence he calls himself the Son of man rather than the Son of God.
28_marg492: The speech by which he signifies, though obscurely, that he is God, as: “I and the Father are one”, and the like. In short, hiding his Godhead and putting forward his manhood, he says: “Whom do men say that the Son of man is?” To which Peter, having searched out the speech: “Thou art Christ, the Son of the living God.” And he earned no small glory for his searching, for at once he heard: “Blessed art thou, Simon Bar-Jona: because flesh and blood,” etc.
28_interl1532: the knowledge of the apostles passes beyond our frailty
28_marg493: The heaven above, etc. As the height of heaven and the depth of the earth cannot be known by men, so the knowledge of the apostles and prophets, who knew the secrets of the Godhead by the revealing of the Spirit, passes beyond our frailty.
28_interl1535: out of the fineness of the letter and of the figurative ceremonies
28_marg494: Take away wickedness, etc. Take away the wickedness of persecuting Christians from the mind of Saul and the like, and when they begin to preach Christ, the chair of their teaching will be established with justice, which before their wickedness was driving to ruin, when, resisting the justice of God, they wished to set up their own.
28_marg495: Take away wickedness, etc. Those who rule the people, if they want their throne to be firm, should always show faces full of cheerfulness and grace, lest by stiff arrogance they incur the hatred of the people.
28_marg496: As above he warned the ruler, now he warns the subject: the one to show a cheerful face to those under him, the other not to appear arrogant in the sight of his betters but, placed in a middle place, to deserve to be called up higher. Whence: “When thou art invited to a wedding, sit down in the lowest place.” In the king and prince can be understood the Lord, in whose sight we must always be humbled. Whence: “Be you humbled under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in the time of visitation.”
28_interl1537: “If thy brother shall offend against thee, go, and rebuke him between thee and him alone.”
28_marg497: Apples of gold, etc. The holy utterances are compared to beds because they prepare rest.
28_marg498: An earring of gold, etc. The humble hearer is rightly compared to an earring of gold, because while he gladly lends his ear to one who rebukes and teaches him, he is already preparing himself to receive the brightness of heavenly wisdom, already drawing near to the vision of the light above.
28_marg499: The learned master is like a bright pearl, because while he opens the amendment of morals and the knowledge of things above to those who devoutly seek them, he adds, as it were, to the golden ornament the greater and more pleasing brightness of a glowing gem.
28_interl1539: in the time of preaching, amid the heats of the persecutors
28_interl1540: “The harvest indeed is great, but the labourers are few.”
28_marg500: As the cold of snow, etc. It seems untimely for it to snow at harvest time. For later too: “As snow in summer, and rain in harvest, so glory is not seemly for a fool.” Yet in hot Palestine it is no small delight if a sudden cold comes, as it does with snow, to cool at times the burning of the sun, wipe away the sweat of labour, and temper burning breath. To this the faithful messenger is well likened, who gives rest to the mind of him who sent him by acting prudently.
28_marg501: This seems the same as: “Deceive not any man with thy lips.” But that means: do not take a man up by promising and deceive him by not fulfilling. This is both the same and what the Apostle says: “Having an appearance indeed of godliness, but denying the power thereof.”
28_interl1544: by bearing what is inflicted for sins
28_interl1550: the sweetness of heavenly understanding, which is made ready by the work of the bees, that is, of the fathers
28_interl1551: “Not to be more wise than it behoveth to be wise.”
28_interl1554: thou lose what thou hadst understood well
28_marg502: Thou hast found honey, etc. It can also be understood as he says plainly afterwards: Withdraw thy foot from the house of thy neighbour. For even if thou find anyone’s talk or visits sweeter than honey, it is better by coming more rarely to make him love thy coming, than either to stay with him so long at one time or to come to him so often that he grows weary.
28_marg503: A rotten tooth, etc. Jeremias: “Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm.” He is rightly compared to a rotten tooth and a weary foot, because he knows not the one good of man, that is, “to adhere to God and put his hope in God”, and can neither take the food of life nor reach the dwelling of the salvation he desires. And he loseth his garment in cold weather, because, though in the calm of the present life he seems clothed in the habit of religion, in the day of judgement he will be shown naked.
28_interl1555: “Blessed is he that keepeth his garments, lest he walk naked.”
28_marg504: Vinegar upon nitre, etc. Nitre is named from the province of Nitria, where it is usually found, and it does not differ much from the appearance of sal ammoniac. For as the heat of the sun makes salt on the seashore by hardening into stones the sea waters which the force of the winds or the surge of the sea casts on the shore, so in Nitria, where the long rains of summer soak the ground, the excessive heat boils the waters into a stone very like salt or ice, yet having nothing of icy cold, nothing of salty taste; which, however, after the nature of salt, usually stays hard in the heat and flows and melts in cloudy air.
28_marg505: The natives use it for washing. Whence: “Though thou wash thyself with nitre, and multiply to thyself the herb borith, thou art stained in thy iniquity.” It crackles in water like quicklime and wastes away, but makes the water fit for washing.
28_interl1557: a perverse mind is kindled to worse by correction
28_marg506: Hot coals, that is, the ardour of charity. For wisdom would not teach thee to do good to an enemy for the sake of harm; for it often happens that an enemy, overcome by repeated kindnesses, lays aside the stiffness of hatred and puts the warmth of charity into his mind.
28_marg507: If thou listen to a detracter with a cheerful face, thou givest him fuel for detraction. But if with a sad one, as someone says, he learns not to say gladly what he has learned is not gladly heard.
28_interl1560: free and apart, in the height of the virtues, from the desires of the world and the bonds of a wife
28_interl1561: to be assailed through carnal pleasure by the daily insults of a wicked woman
28_marg508: It is better, etc. A housetop is a high and secret place. For in the Acts of the Apostles, where Peter went up to the upper parts to pray, for “the upper parts” “housetop” is written in the Greek.
28_marg509: As cold water, etc. “As the hart panteth after the fountains of water; so my soul panteth after thee, O God.” Cold water, then, which quenches the burning of the thirsty, and a messenger who brings from far off news of unlooked-for joys, are likened together, because both the sweetness of the divine vision consoles the soul that has long desired it and frees it from the heat of tribulation; and daily the angels, coming down into the world from a far country, that is, from the heavenly fatherland, either strengthen the just amid temptations with the hope of heavenly things or, the contest finished, lead them to the palm of reward.
28_interl1562: “The mouth of the just shall meditate wisdom: and his tongue shall speak judgment.”
28_marg510: A fountain troubled, etc. It often happens that those who shone with greater knowledge, wishing at last to know more than is granted to human frailty, fall into the pit of folly. Whence he adds: As it is not good for a man to eat much honey, etc. For the sweetness of honey, if more is taken than ought to be, kills the eater by what delights him. Sweet too is the searching of majesty, but he who searches beyond measure is overwhelmed by its glory; because, like honey taken immoderately, it bursts the sense of the searcher, since it is not contained. And not only must every wise man attend to this, but also that he not make useless by immoderate speech what he could rightly and usefully know. Whence he adds: As a city that lieth open, etc.
28_marg511: For if the city of the mind has no wall of silence, it lies open to the darts of the enemy; and when it throws itself out of itself through words, it shows itself open to the adversary, who overcomes it the more easily as the city that is conquered fights against itself by much speaking.
28_interl1564: let not the honour of teaching be entrusted to the unlearned
28_marg512: As snow, etc. Snow in summer and rain in harvest are the persecutions of the unbelievers in the time of preaching, which, when they press the more heavily, both hinder the warmth of love in many and spoil the crops of good work. To these the glory of a fool is compared, because if the chair of teaching is given to an unlearned man, the Church is harmed by this just as by the persecution of unbelievers; as the disaster of the Arian storm proved.
28_marg513: As a bird, etc. He compares words to birds, because they fly through the air from the mouth of the speaker to the hearer. But a bird often settles where there is no use or need; words, however, do not vanish scattered into the wind, but all return to their author, and either help the speaker if well spoken or weigh him down if ill, so that we shall be made to render account in the day of judgement for every idle word. How much more do curses, not only those maliciously hurled at the innocent but also those carelessly uttered everywhere against anyone, weigh down not another but the curser himself: “Nor railers shall possess the kingdom of God.” And not without cause he adds: a curse uttered without cause. The way of a ship in the sea is the way of iniquity, which, driven by the blasts of the devil through the bitter waves of the world, runs with such subtlety that its track can scarcely or never be detected. 28_marg583: And thy riches, etc. That is, do not corrupt the hearts of men with earthly delights, lest they seek the heavenly things in which they may reign for ever with the Lord. For kings are destroyed by riches when those united by faith to the body of the highest king deserve, through the allurements of the world, to be rooted out of the land of the living.
28_marg584: Give not to kings, etc. These and the following are plain according to the letter. But allegorically he commands that the minds of the faithful, who are members of the eternal king, be not made drunk with wine, in which is lust; because there is no secret where drunkenness reigneth: nothing of heavenly things is thought of where carnal pleasure reigns, but carnal men search out only the things that are visible.
28_interl1695: of the allurements of the flesh
28_interl1697: of Christ, who was poor for us
28_marg585: Give strong drink to them that are sad, etc. Wine and strong drink are the consolation of divine wisdom, which is owed to those who refuse to be consoled in low things and receive with a bitter mind whatever befalls them in the present, cleaving with all their mind to heavenly things. Whence: “My soul refused to be comforted: I remembered God, and was delighted.” Again: Give strong drink, etc.: namely to the penitent, who are weighed down by grief and sadness for their former deeds; pour abundantly into them the gladness of spiritual knowledge, like “wine that maketh glad the heart of man”, lest such be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow.
28_marg586: Remember to speak thyself for the cause of the poor man who cannot speak for himself in judgement, and defend those who, looking to the heavenly fatherland, pass the more quickly along the way of this life. Or: to open thy mouth for the dumb is to preach the word of preaching to the gentiles, who before did not know how to sound forth the divine utterances, and to spend care for salvation not only on the Jews but on all nations throughout the world.
28_marg587: As he commanded thee to open thy mouth for the cause and rescue of the poor, so he warns thee to chastise and judge justly where he has erred. And Moses: “Neither shalt thou favour a poor man in judgment.” Both of which the prophet says the Lord does: “But he shall judge the poor with justice, and shall reprove with equity for the meek of the earth.”

28_marg588: Thus far the words of king Lamuel. From here Solomon sings the praises of the Church in a few verses but with the fullest truth. For this song consists of twenty-two verses in the order of the Hebrew alphabet, and each verse begins with its own letter; by which it is hinted how fully the virtues and rewards are described here, either of each faithful soul or of the whole holy Church, which is made one catholic Church out of all the elect. Who shall find a valiant woman? etc. The valiant woman is holy Church, because she bears spiritual children to God “of water and the Spirit”. Valiant, because she despises all the adversity or prosperity of the world for the love of God; whom he, appearing in the flesh, found weak and made strong. Whence, returning to heaven, he says to the angels: “Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that was lost.” Solomon, then, seeing the human race entangled in countless errors, and that none suffices for its salvation but “the one mediator of God and men”, says: Who shall find a valiant woman? etc.; as if he openly marvelled at the grace of God to come. Who is such, who so great, as to gather to himself out of so many unbelieving nations of the world the one Church of the elect, and make her valiant and invincible by his grace? Not one like us, not of our time, but God, who at the end of the ages would become man, to redeem us from death by his passion. For this is what he says: far and from the uttermost coasts is the price of her. Far, by the interval of time from Solomon to the virgin’s childbearing; from the uttermost coasts, because “his going out is from the end of heaven”. For he gave no other price for us than himself. Whence: “Who loved us, and delivered himself for us,” etc. Though it can also rightly be understood thus: the price of holy Church was set far off, because the incarnation of the Word, his life among men, his passion and resurrection, are far removed from our nature. For he was born when he would and of what mother he would, and lived in the world without sin, and died when and how he would, and rose and ascended when he would, and the like, in which he is “as far from us as heaven from earth”. And because the Lord granted to the Church he redeemed not only to receive the word of salvation but also to fight constantly for it and preach it through the world, he adds: The heart of her husband trusteth in her. The husband is the Redeemer; whence: “For I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.” What he says, then, The heart of her husband trusteth in her, is drawn from a human likeness. For as he who has a strong, faithful and chaste wife trusts in her, because she does nothing against his will and is not defiled even by the thought of adultery, will gladly bear all things for love of him, and will turn whom she can to friendship with him, so God trusts in the Church. For he knows the Spirit of grace which he gave, knows the strength of charity which he poured into her heart. And so he does not doubt that she not only cannot be corrupted from the soundness of her faith, but will also press on perseveringly to gather more to the knowledge and unity of the faith. And this is: he shall have no need of spoils. For the Church spoils the devil when, through her preachers, she calls to the truth those whom he had deceived.
28_marg589: Because the Church will never cease to restore to the faith of Christ the souls deceived by the devil, until, the course of the world finished, the number of the just is complete. But because whatever good holy Church or the faithful soul does it receives from above, it is rightly added: She will render him good, and not evil, all the days of her life. The soul renders good to Christ when it answers the gifts of life it has received by living rightly, and strives to make known to others what it knows or does. And when he has said, she will render him good, he adds, and not evil, because some, having received good things from God, repay evil: either they turn into heresy the mysteries of faith they have received, or deny in deeds the faith they confess in words, or corrupt good morals by evil talk, or do not persevere to the end in a good purpose. Whence, when he had said, she will render him good, and not evil, to show that perseverance is necessary he added: all the days of her life. Like which: “That we may serve him in holiness and justice before him, all our days.”
28_marg590: To what works, to what fruits of justice or holiness he who seeks to repay what he receives should rather apply himself, he says thus: She hath sought wool and flax, etc. This holy Church does even according to the letter, following that saying: “When thou shalt see one naked, cover him, and despise not thy own flesh.” And she works not thoughtlessly but with counsel, that she may earn to hear from her husband Christ in the judgement: “I was naked, and you covered me”, and: “As long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me.” Of her hands: that is, of those persons through whom she gives alms to the poor; in whose devout work she uses most wholesome counsel, so that when “he hath distributed, he hath given to the poor”, it may be not to be praised by men for a time, but that “his justice remaineth for ever and ever”.
28_marg591: Mystically, in wool, which is the covering of sheep, we take the works of devotion and simplicity that are spent on our neighbours. In flax, which springs green from the earth but by much and long working loses its native moisture and comes to the grace of a new whiteness, we take the chastening of our flesh. For while we burn out by continence the inborn filth of the vices, we make a worthy garment in which to put on Christ. Whence: “For as many of you as have been baptized in Christ, have put on Christ.” The valiant woman, then, seeks wool and flax and works by the counsel of her hands when the Church anxiously searches with what fruits of devotion she may exercise herself and how she may cleanse herself of fleshly allurements; and this with most prudent counsel, that is, looking only to the reward from above. Of this reward it is added more plainly: She is like the merchant’s ship, she bringeth her bread from afar. The sailor is called a merchant because he presses diligently on with acquiring wares. As, then, the merchant’s ship carries over the sea, laden, the wares that abound in his own country, so that, having sold what he brought, he may carry home dearer things, so the Church, so the perfect soul, rejoices to be laden with the riches of the virtues, by which to buy the greater gifts of divine grace. For it is the best trade when, doing the good we can, we first receive from the Lord this reward, that we always advance to doing greater things, and then eternal life. So the holy soul, like a merchant’s ship, which crosses the waves of the world by desire, thinks only of the joys it hopes for in heaven, does whatever it can with earnestness to gain the eternal ones more abundantly, and strives to hope for them in whatever adversity befalls it. She bringeth her bread from afar, because in all she does she awaits only the eternal reward, and desires only to be filled with the living bread, who says: “Come to me, all you that labour, and are burdened, and I will refresh you.” He receives his bread near at hand who, in what he does justly, seeks only the rewards of human favour, with no regard to eternal life; of whom it is said: “Amen I say to you, they have received their reward.”
28_marg592: And she hath risen in the night, etc. As the whole course of the present world varies by day and night, and the day is for working, the night for resting, so the time of the Church is divided into a twofold state of rest and work. For she rests, as it were, by night when the faithful man, laying aside the cares of the world, begins to be at leisure for himself and to care for himself spiritually, or to exercise himself in secret with readings, prayers, tears and the like.
28_marg593: And she rises in the night when a faithful man girds himself diligently to take care of his neighbours. This he does in two ways: he calls to the faith those who stray outside, and rouses those who are in the faith to apply themselves more to works. Whence he adds: and given a prey to her household, and victuals to her maidens.
28_marg594: She gives a prey to her household when she joins those whom she has snatched from the devil to the fellowship of those who went before in the faith.
28_marg595: She gives victuals to her maidens when she refreshes the humble, and those who keep the commands out of fear, with the remembrance of the reward, lest they grow faint in their devout labour.
28_marg596: Today and until the end of the world the valiant woman hath considered a field, and bought it: with the fruit of her hands she hath planted a vineyard; because the Church always seeks out whom she may convert to the faith, and those whom she finds teachable she buys for the service of Christ with the money of the Word, and takes care to plant the vineyard of Christ in them, or rather to make them the vineyard of Christ. And because he who desires to teach another ought first to abstain from evil and do good works, he adds: She hath girded her loins with strength.
28_marg597: The field is the possession of the inheritance above. Of which: “Behold, the smell of my son is as the smell of a plentiful field, which the Lord hath blessed.” For the fragrance of the saints is “as the smell of a plentiful field, which the Lord hath blessed”, because with the whole intent of the mind they behold what is the fulness of blessedness in the kingdom of God. The Church, then, hath considered a field, and bought it with the fruit of her hands, because she has studiously learned what are the joys of life, and labours for them as much as she can.
28_marg598: Because out of the fruitful deeds or words of her faithful she put together the Scripture with which to make her hearers drunk with faith and love. And by the vineyard we rightly take the Church, which is denoted by the valiant woman, and by the shoots of the vineyard those who are the children of the woman. And the woman planted the vineyard when the early Church, sending preachers through the world, scattered the seeds of the faith. For she considered the field, that is, the world, bristling with the thorns of the vices and needing a spiritual husbandman. She bought it when she gave the talent of the word to her hearers, so as to make believers over to Christ. And she planted the vineyard in that same field when she established among the new peoples of believers a Church full of the gospel’s teaching. This vineyard she planted with the fruit of her hands, because the saints taught those whom they instructed not only by word but by deeds and miracles.
28_interl1712: when, intent on heavenly desires, she scorns to give way to fleshly allurements
28_marg599: When she prepares herself for the works of the virtues, she rightly first girds her loins and then strengthens her arm; because a good work is not acceptable to God unless the lust of flesh and mind is first restrained. Whence: “Cease to do perversely, learn to do well”; and: “Let your loins be girt, and lamps burning in your hands”, that you may shine with good works.
28_interl1713: good, once the world is shut out
28_marg600: The traffic, namely, of that field of which it was said: She hath considered a field, and bought it. Holy Church, then, and the perfect soul, hath tasted, that is, has known by the great desire of the mind, that good is the traffic of the unfading life, which, the world forsaken, earns eternal life in heaven. She hath tasted, that is, has learned openly that it is good, by earnestness in preaching, to lead whomever she can to the way of truth. And therefore the lamp of her devotion cannot be put out by any darkness of tribulations, nor by death itself. For the lamp of those is put out in the night who, though they seem to burn in the day, believe for a while and in time of temptation fall away. But the lamp of those is put out at midnight who, at the coming of the judge, are proved not to have had the oil of charity in the vessels of their hearts, when, the fame of their false virtues lost, they pay the true torments of their dark deeds. But if in this place we take the night for rest, as above, And she hath risen in the night, that is, she made herself ready for working after rest, it is plainly said that the lamp of holy Church is not put out in the night, because even when she rests from action she is the more free for contemplation, and when she ceases from public works she applies herself the more ardently to readings or to the divine praises; like a woman who not only presses on with her labours in the day, but works with her hands at night too by the light of a lamp.
28_marg601: She hath put out her hand, etc. By strong things he means works perfect in charity, in which the Church exercises herself for the eternal reward. Whence: “Do good to them that hate you”, and: “If thou wilt be perfect, go sell what thou hast, and give to the poor.” For the synagogue, to which it is said: “If you be willing, and will hearken to me, you shall eat the good things of the land”, is the weaker in the work of justice the less it is raised up by hope of the eternal reward. But the Church, which hears: “Do penance: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand”, rightly bears all things for this reward or recompense. Of whose strength it is said: “The kingdom of heaven suffereth violence, and the violent bear it away.” And her fingers, he says, have taken hold of the spindle. The distaff is in the left hand, the spindle in the right. The wool passes from the distaff by the thread to the spindle. The right hand signifies eternal life, the left the present gifts of God, that is, plenty of goods, peace, health, the knowledge of the Scriptures, of the heavenly commands and of the sacraments. When we receive these and the like from God we carry, as it were, wool on the distaff in the left hand. But when we begin to practise them wholesomely for the love of heavenly things, we pass the wool of the spotless Lamb from the distaff to the spindle, from the left hand to the right, as we make for ourselves, from the gifts of our Redeemer and the examples of his works, the robe of heavenly glory and the wedding garment of charity. For the fingers with which she takes hold of the spindle signify the purpose of discretion with which each one works, because no members of the body are so divided by joints and bends. Those, then, whose conversation is in heaven, whence also we look for the Saviour: their right fingers have taken hold of the spindle, because they labour with careful discretion for eternal things. And it is well said, have taken hold of the spindle, that we may learn with how much zeal, how much haste, we ought to act. And what the valiant woman, namely holy Church or the perfect soul, has wrought with the spindle he adds: She hath opened her hand to the needy, and stretched out her hands, etc.
28_marg602: She hath opened her hand, etc. This can be taken of the alms that are given to the poor, but better of the word of God, which bestows the garment of salvation on souls. Whence Job: “I was clad with justice: and I clothed myself with my judgment, as with a robe and a diadem.” She opened her hand to the needy when she reveals the mysteries of the faith to the ignorant through the workmen of the truth; she stretched out her hands to the poor when she scattered preachers far and wide to the nations that lacked eternal salvation.
28_interl1716: a serving heart, or a heart of service
28_marg603: The cold of snow is the hearts of the wicked, stiff with the numbness of faithlessness. Of which: “And because iniquity hath abounded, the charity of many shall grow cold.” These are weighed down by that snow which, falling through pride from heaven into darkness, still presumes to show itself like an angel of light, and puts forward a snow-white habit, which belongs to God and his angels: namely to signify the brightness of their virtue by a snowy habit. But she shall not fear for her house in the cold of snow, because she believed God, who said that “the gates of hell shall not prevail against” it. For all her domestics are clothed with double garments: with wisdom, namely, to lay heresies bare, and with patience to bear the attacks of open enemies. Or clothed with double garments, because they have the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come: now helped by God so as not to fail, then enriched in blessedness by the divine vision. Again, clothed with double garments, one of the body, the other of the mind: with faith and deeds, steeped in the sacraments and the examples of their Redeemer. Whence: “As many of you as have been baptized in Christ, have put on Christ.”
28_marg604: The cold of snow can also be understood as the eternal torments, which are mixed of fire and cold. Whence: “There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” For weeping comes from fire and smoke, gnashing from cold. Whence Job: “Let him pass from the snow waters to excessive heat.” But the Church shall not fear these for her house, because whoever perish did not belong to her house, nor were clothed with her spiritual garment. For in the gospel it is said of him who had not the wedding garment: “Bind his hands and feet, and cast him into the exterior darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” He is rightly bound in the cold, because he had not the garment of devotion.
28_marg605: Clothing of tapestry, etc. Tapestry clothing, which is usually made with varied weaving, signifies the very firm and strong works of the Church and the diverse ornaments of her virtues; of which: “The queen stood on thy right hand,” etc. Fine linen is the chastity of a pure conscience and life; purple, the shedding of blood. For fine linen is of a white colour; the colour purple too comes from the blood of a creature, for what is called purple is made from it and has the look of blood. Therefore holy Church is said to have lilies in peace, roses in war. Again, because fine linen springs up green but, losing its native moisture by much working, is brought to the beauty of a white garment, the Church is clothed with fine linen when the elect chasten their bodies; and with purple, which belongs to kings, when they practise continence not for love of praise but of the everlasting kingdom. To her: “Let us be glad and rejoice, and give glory to him; for the marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath prepared herself. And it is granted to her that she should clothe herself with fine linen, glittering and white. For the fine linen are the justifications of saints.”
28_marg606: Her husband is honourable in the gates, etc. The husband is the Lord, who was seen without honour when he stood before the tribunal to be judged, but will be honourable when he comes to judge, “and all the angels with him,” etc. In the gates, because the men of old sat in the gates to judge, so that those who came might at once receive the judge’s ready answer, and the unaccustomed buildings of the city might not amaze countryfolk or shepherds, nor the frequent dispute of litigants spoil the peace of the city. The Lord, then, will be honourable in the gates of his city, because he who is now despised by many, when the end of the world comes and he opens the entrance of the heavenly fatherland to the elect, will appear on high to all.
28_marg607: In the cloth of fine linen is the delicate weaving of holy preaching, in which one rests softly, because in it we are cherished by heavenly hope. Whence too the animals are shown to Peter in a linen sheet, because the souls of sinners, mercifully gathered together, are held in the gentle rest of faith. This fine linen, then, the Church made and sold, because the faith which she had woven by believing she gave by speaking, and received from unbelievers a life of right conduct. And she delivered a girdle to the Chanaanite, because by the vigour of the justice she showed she bound up the loose works of the gentiles, so that by living they might keep what is commanded: “Let your loins be girt.” For by Chanaan the gentiles are meant, from whom also they descend; and Chanaan is interpreted “changed”. For the gentiles have passed from the vices to the virtues, from the devil to Christ. Whence: “For them that shall be changed, for the sons of Core, … a canticle for the beloved”; and afterwards: “Forget thy people and thy father’s house.”
28_marg608: Strength, etc. Strength for bearing, beauty for practising the grace of the virtues. Beauty because she works justice; strength because she “suffereth persecution for justice’ sake”. And therefore she shall laugh in the latter day, that is, she will rejoice in the reward of the heavenly kingdom, who grieved in the contest of the present life. “Blessed are ye that weep now: for you shall laugh.” And Job: “Till thy mouth be filled with laughter.” Like this the prophet says of the Lord: “The Lord hath reigned, he is clothed with beauty: the Lord is clothed with strength, and hath girded himself.” When he preached the gospel of the kingdom he pleased some and displeased others. Towards those whom he pleased he put on beauty; towards those whom he displeased, strength. Do thou too imitate the Lord thy God, that thou mayst be his garment. Be with beauty towards those whom thy works please; be strong against detracters.
28_marg609: She hath opened her mouth, etc. When she speaks she opened her mouth only to teach wisdom, according to that saying: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth; but that which is good, to the edification of faith, that it may administer grace to the hearers.” Or she opened the mouth of her heart to learn within, from wisdom itself, the truth she would teach outwardly. To both agrees what he adds: and the law of clemency is on her tongue.
28_marg610: So as not to punish at once, like the law of Moses, but to spare mercifully. As the Lord said of the sinful woman: “He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her”; and so he absolved her: “Go, and now sin no more.”
28_marg611: She hath looked well, etc. Because she subtly searches out all the thoughts of her conscience. She hath not eaten her bread idle, because she carries out in deed the holy word she receives. Again, the house of the valiant woman is the dwelling of the heavenly fatherland; the paths are the precepts of justice by which one comes to the mansion of life; which the soul looks well to when it both diligently considers by what acts it should reach heaven and does not cease to practise what it has learned is to be done. She hath not eaten her bread idle when, receiving the body of the Lord, she strives to imitate in act what she celebrates in mystery, lest by eating the bread of the Lord and drinking the chalice unworthily she eat and drink judgement to herself. Or it can be taken simply that she hath not eaten her bread idle, according to that saying: “If any man will not work, neither let him eat.” And Paul himself of himself: “For such things as were needful for me and them that are with me, these hands have furnished.” Whence, rebuking wanton widows, he says: “And withal being idle they learn to go about from house to house: and are not only idle, but tattlers also, and busybodies.”
28_marg612: Her children rose up, etc. What he knew would come to pass he tells, like a prophet, as already done. The children of the Church will rise, that is, the elect, immortal; and then they will proclaim most blessed the mother who bore them “of water and the Holy Ghost”, who is now despised as though wretched, as the Apostle says: “If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable.” But we who fight for another life will rightly, when it shall appear what we shall be, proclaim our mother most blessed.
28_marg613: This also, Her children rose up, and called her most blessed, can be taken even now, when one of the faithful, having passed beyond the hardships of the world, is led to heaven. For sometimes sitting belongs to humiliation, rising to glory. Whence it is said of the Ninevites in the gospel: “They had long ago done penance, sitting in sackcloth and ashes”; and: “Rise ye after you have sitten, you that eat the bread of sorrow.” The children of the Church rise, then, and proclaim her most blessed when, raised to the heavenly goods, they see how great that blessedness is and celebrate it with due praise. Her husband praises her when he rewards the good things he himself gave. And with what words he praises her he shows: Many daughters have gathered together.
28_marg614: Her husband too will rise and praise her in the judgement, saying: “Come, ye blessed of my Father,” etc. He indeed, the firstfruits of them that sleep, rose from the dead; but in the judgement he will show how great is the glory of his resurrection.
28_marg615: Many daughters, etc. The churches of the heretics and of wicked catholics, which are called daughters either of Christ or of the Church, because they are not far removed from the Lord’s sacraments, and received “the adoption of sons”, which they did not keep. Whence John: “They went out from us, but they were not of us.” They have gathered together riches, good works, namely fasts, alms, affliction and the like, which are the true riches of the spirit where they are done with pure sincerity of mind, but without faith profit nothing. And those daughters too gather riches in vain of whom it is said: “Many will say to me in that day: Lord, Lord, have not we … cast out devils in thy name, and done many miracles in thy name? And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you.” But the Church surpasses these daughters, who follows the footsteps of her Redeemer with chaste faith and perfect work.
28_marg616: Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain, etc. Deceitful is the glory of praise that the soul receives from man; vain the beauty of chastity or of good working that a soul without the fear of God shows off to men. But that conscience is truly worthy of praise which keeps the fear of God in all things. For it is the beginning of wisdom and the guardian of the virtues. Whence: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” And elsewhere: “He that feareth God, neglecteth nothing.” Hence it is that Job both flourished in virtues in prosperity and remained invincible in adversity, because he truly said: “For I have always feared God as waves swelling over me, and his weight I was not able to bear.” Deceitful, then, is the favour of hypocrites, vain the beauty of the work of fools. But the Church, which lives in fear in the exile of this world, because she offers burning lamps of virtues to the bridegroom coming to judgement, rightly praised by him, will enter with him the door of the heavenly kingdom. How he praises her he shows: Give her of the fruit.
28_marg617: Give her of the fruit of her hands, etc. This is that husband of whom it was said above, her husband, and he praised her; who at the end will command the angels to bring the Church, after the contest of this life, after the threshing of afflictions, into the joys of the kingdom, and to join her to himself as partner of immortal life, according to this: “But the wheat gather ye into my barn.” Give her of the fruit of her hands, because she took care to bear the fruit of the Spirit, “charity, joy, peace,” etc. And let them praise her in the gates, namely in the judgement, or at the entrance of the heavenly fatherland: not the empty favours of men, but her own works which she did, God examining, approving and rewarding them; to whom be honour and glory.
